title: Weather & Climate
description: The difference between weather and climate — how we measure the elements of weather, cloud types, the three types of rainfall, weather maps, air pressure and wind, and microclimates.

notes.heading: Weather and Climate
notes.body: Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time — it can change within minutes or hours. Climate is the average weather of a place measured over a long period, usually 30 years or more. A useful saying: 'Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.' A place can have a hot, dry summer climate yet still experience one cold, wet day — that day is weather, the overall pattern is climate. Weather is described using elements: temperature, precipitation, wind speed and direction, air pressure, cloud cover, humidity and sunshine. Climate matters because it shapes whole ways of life: what crops farmers can grow, how houses are built (steep roofs where snow falls, flat roofs in dry lands), what clothes people wear, and where tourists travel. Different parts of the world have very different climate zones — tropical, desert, temperate, Mediterranean, polar — each defined by its long-term temperature and rainfall patterns. Scientists study climate using long records of weather data collected at weather stations over decades.

notes.heading: Measuring the Weather: Instruments
notes.body: Each element of weather is measured with a specific instrument. Temperature is measured with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius (°C); a maximum-minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperatures over 24 hours. Air pressure is measured with a barometer, in millibars (mb) or hectopascals (hPa); rising pressure usually means settled, fine weather, falling pressure often means storms. Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge — a funnel collecting rain into a measuring cylinder, read in millimetres (mm). Wind speed is measured with an anemometer (cups that spin in the wind), in kilometres per hour or on the Beaufort scale; wind direction is shown by a wind vane or windsock, and winds are named after the direction they blow FROM — a 'westerly' comes from the west. Sunshine hours are recorded by a sunshine recorder, and humidity (moisture in the air) by a hygrometer. For fair, comparable readings, instruments are kept in a Stevenson screen — a white, louvered, slatted box on legs, about 1.25 m above grass. The white paint reflects sunlight, the slats allow air to flow through, and the height keeps readings above ground-level heat. Measurements should be taken at the same times each day.

notes.heading: Cloud Types
notes.body: Clouds form when moist air rises, cools, and its water vapour condenses into tiny droplets around dust particles. Clouds are classified by their height and shape, and their names come from Latin words: cirrus (curl of hair) — high, wispy, feather-like clouds made of ice crystals, often the first sign of an approaching weather system; cumulus (heap) — white, fluffy, heaped clouds with flat bases, like cotton wool; stratus (layer) — low, grey, flat sheets covering the sky like a blanket; nimbus (rain) — added to a name to mean rain-bearing. The main types: Cirrus — high and wispy; usually fair weather but can warn of approaching rain. Cumulus — fluffy fair-weather clouds; fine conditions. Cumulonimbus — giant towering 'anvil-topped' storm clouds bringing heavy showers, thunder, lightning and hail. Stratus — low grey layer giving dull skies and light drizzle. Nimbostratus — thick dark rain sheet bringing long, steady rain. Altocumulus — mid-level patchy white-grey rolls or ripples. A simple weather rule: high thin clouds = watch for change; fluffy small clouds = fine; low dark layered clouds = rain; towering dark clouds = storms.

notes.heading: The Three Types of Rainfall
notes.body: All rainfall happens because air rises and cools, and its water vapour condenses — but there are three different triggers that force air upwards. Relief (orographic) rainfall: moist wind blows towards hills or mountains and is forced to rise. The air cools, condenses into clouds, and rain falls on the windward slope. On the far (leeward) side the air descends, warms and dries, creating a dry rain shadow. This is why the west of Britain, facing moist Atlantic winds over western hills, is much wetter than the east. Convectional rainfall: on hot days the Sun heats the ground, which warms the air above it. Warm air rises rapidly in strong currents (convection), cools, and condenses into towering cumulonimbus clouds — producing short, heavy afternoon thunderstorms, common in summer and in tropical regions every afternoon. Frontal rainfall: where a mass of warm air meets a mass of cold air (a front), the lighter warm air is forced to rise up and over the denser cold air. As it rises it cools and condenses, producing a broad band of steady rain — the typical drizzle-then-rain sequence as a warm front passes over the UK. Key point: in every type, the essential sequence is rise → cool → condense → rain.

notes.heading: Weather Maps and Symbols
notes.body: Weather maps (synoptic charts) summarise conditions over a whole country at one moment. Lines called isobars join places with equal air pressure, with the value in millibars — just as contours join points of equal height. Where isobars are close together, pressure changes rapidly over a short distance and winds are strong; widely spaced isobars mean light winds. High pressure areas (anticyclones, marked H) bring settled weather: clear skies, light winds, dry — hot and sunny in summer, cold and frosty with fog in winter. Low pressure areas (depressions, marked L) bring unsettled weather: strong winds, cloud and rain as air rises. Fronts are lines showing where air masses meet: a warm front (red semicircles) brings steady rain then warmer conditions; a cold front (blue triangles) brings short, heavy showers then cooler, clearer air; an occluded front (both symbols) is where a cold front has overtaken a warm front. Wind direction arrows point the way the wind blows; wind strength is shown by 'feathers' on the arrow shaft — each full feather is about 10 knots. Station symbols also record temperature, cloud cover (how much of a circle is shaded) and current weather such as rain or snow.

notes.heading: Air Pressure and Wind
notes.body: Air has weight — the atmosphere presses down on us, and this is air pressure, measured in millibars with a barometer. Average sea-level pressure is about 1013 mb; above roughly 1020 mb is high pressure, below about 1000 mb is low. Air pressure depends on whether air is rising or sinking. Low pressure forms where air is heated and rises: rising air means less weight pressing down, and as the air ascends it cools, condenses and forms clouds — so lows bring wind, cloud and rain. High pressure forms where air cools and sinks: sinking air is compressed and warms slightly, so clouds evaporate and skies clear — highs bring calm, dry, settled weather. Wind is simply air moving from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure — like air rushing out of a punctured tyre. The bigger the pressure difference (the closer the isobars), the faster the wind. Winds are named by the direction they come FROM: a southerly wind blows from the south and usually brings warm air to the UK, while a northerly brings cold Arctic air. In the northern hemisphere, winds blow anticlockwise around a low and clockwise around a high.

notes.heading: Microclimates
notes.body: A microclimate is the climate of a very small area — a garden, a street, a playground — which can differ noticeably from the surrounding area. Microclimates exist because local features modify temperature, wind, shade and shelter. Examples: South-facing slopes (in the northern hemisphere) receive more direct sunshine, so they are warmer and better for growing crops like grapes; north-facing slopes stay cooler and damper. Buildings and walls: a wall facing the sun absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, creating a warm, sheltered strip beside it — gardeners use this for tender plants. Cities create an urban microclimate called the urban heat island: roads and buildings store heat, traffic releases it, and tall buildings block cooling winds, so city centres can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. Trees provide shade and shelter — under a tree it is cooler in summer and winds are weaker all year. Wind tunnel effects: gaps between tall buildings funnel and speed up wind, making some street corners much windier. Aspect, altitude, surface type (dark tarmac heats faster than grass) and water (lakes and ponds keep nearby air cooler in summer and milder in winter) all create microclimates. Understanding microclimates helps farmers choose crops, gardeners choose plants, and architects design comfortable buildings.

flashcards.definition: The day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a place — temperature, rainfall, wind, pressure and cloud — changing over hours or days.
flashcards.example: This morning was frosty but by afternoon it was warm and sunny.

flashcards.definition: The average weather of a place measured over a long period, usually at least 30 years.
flashcards.example: The Sahara has a hot, dry climate even though a rare storm may bring rain on one day.

flashcards.definition: The instrument that measures air temperature in degrees Celsius; a maximum-minimum type records the day's highest and lowest values.
flashcards.example: A thermometer inside a Stevenson screen reads 18°C at midday.

flashcards.definition: The instrument that measures air pressure in millibars; falling pressure often signals approaching storms.
flashcards.example: The barometer dropped from 1020 mb to 990 mb overnight as a depression arrived.

flashcards.definition: The instrument that measures wind speed, using cups that spin in the wind; wind direction is measured separately with a wind vane.
flashcards.example: The anemometer cups spun rapidly as the storm's wind speed reached 80 km/h.

flashcards.definition: A white, slatted, louvered box on legs that shelters weather instruments so readings are accurate and comparable.
flashcards.example: Its white paint reflects sunlight and the slats let air flow freely around the thermometers inside.

flashcards.definition: A towering, anvil-topped storm cloud formed by powerful rising air currents, bringing heavy showers, thunder and lightning.
flashcards.example: On a hot afternoon, dark cumulonimbus clouds build up and unleash a thunderstorm.

flashcards.definition: Rain caused when moist air is forced to rise over hills or mountains, cooling and condensing; the leeward side lies in a dry rain shadow.
flashcards.example: Western Britain is wetter than the east because Atlantic winds rise over the western hills.

flashcards.definition: Rain caused when the Sun heats the ground, warm air rises rapidly, cools and condenses into storm clouds, producing short heavy downpours.
flashcards.example: Tropical regions get convectional thunderstorms most afternoons after the morning heat builds.

flashcards.definition: The boundary where a warm air mass meets a cold air mass; warm air rises over the cold, causing a band of steady frontal rain.
flashcards.example: A warm front passing overhead brings several hours of steady rain followed by milder air.

flashcards.definition: A line on a weather map joining places of equal air pressure; closely spaced isobars mean strong winds.
flashcards.example: Isobars packed tightly around a depression warned forecasters of gale-force winds.

flashcards.definition: The climate of a very small area that differs from its surroundings because of local features like slopes, walls, trees or buildings.
flashcards.example: A sunny, sheltered spot beside a south-facing wall is warm enough to grow tomatoes.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between weather and climate?
choices: Weather is the long-term average; climate is day-to-day conditions
Weather is day-to-day atmospheric conditions; climate is the average over 30 or more years
Weather only means rainfall; climate only means temperature
There is no difference — they are the same thing
questions.explanation: Weather describes short-term, day-to-day conditions that change within hours. Climate is the long-term average pattern, calculated over at least 30 years.

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure air pressure?
choices: Anemometer
Rain gauge
Barometer
Thermometer
questions.explanation: A barometer measures air pressure in millibars. An anemometer measures wind speed, a rain gauge measures rainfall, and a thermometer measures temperature.

questions.stem: Why are weather instruments kept inside a Stevenson screen?
choices: To make them easier for visitors to see
To keep rain off the instruments so they never get wet
So readings are accurate and comparable: the white surface reflects sunlight, the slats let air flow, and the standard height avoids ground heat
To stop birds nesting on the equipment
questions.explanation: The screen's white paint reflects the Sun, louvered slats allow free air circulation, and its legs hold instruments about 1.25 m above the ground — all so every weather station measures under identical fair conditions.

questions.stem: A towering dark cloud with a flattened 'anvil' top builds up on a hot summer afternoon. What is it, and what weather will it bring?
choices: Cirrus — continuing fine weather
Stratus — light drizzle all day
Cumulonimbus — a short, heavy thunderstorm
Altocumulus — gentle sunshine
questions.explanation: The towering anvil shape is cumulonimbus, formed by powerful convection currents. It produces short, intense downpours with thunder and lightning — classic hot-afternoon convectional storms.

questions.stem: What is the essential sequence that produces ALL types of rainfall?
choices: Air sinks → warms → evaporates → dries
Air rises → cools → water vapour condenses → droplets grow and fall as rain
Wind blows → clouds form → temperature rises → rain
Pressure rises → clouds vanish → rain falls
questions.explanation: Whether the trigger is relief, convection or a front, the mechanism is identical: air is forced up, cooling causes condensation, and the droplets grow heavy enough to fall. Sinking air warms and dries instead, bringing clear skies.

questions.stem: The west of Britain is much wetter than the east. Which type of rainfall explains this, and how?
choices: Convectional — the west is hotter so more storms form
Relief — moist Atlantic winds are forced to rise over western hills, cooling and raining; the east lies in the rain shadow
Frontal — fronts only ever occur in the west
None — it is just chance
questions.explanation: Prevailing south-westerly winds carry moist Atlantic air which rises over the western uplands, producing relief rainfall. Descending air on the eastern (leeward) side warms and dries, leaving the east in a drier rain shadow.

questions.stem: On a synoptic chart, what does closely spaced isobars indicate?
choices: Light winds and calm conditions
Strong winds, because pressure is changing rapidly over a short distance
Warm temperatures
Heavy fog
questions.explanation: Wind is air moving from high to low pressure; the bigger the pressure difference over a distance, the faster it flows. Tightly packed isobars signal a steep pressure gradient and strong winds.

questions.stem: A red line with semicircles on a weather map marks a warm front. What weather sequence does it bring as it passes?
choices: Sudden heavy showers, then much colder air
High cirrus, then thickening cloud, hours of steady rain, then warmer milder conditions
Immediate sunshine with no cloud
Thunder and lightning followed by hail
questions.explanation: At a warm front, warm air rises gently over cold air, so cloud thickens gradually and steady rain falls for hours, followed by the warmer air mass. Sudden heavy showers then colder, clearer air describes a cold front.

questions.stem: Why does high pressure (an anticyclone) usually bring dry, settled weather?
choices: Because air is rising, which cools and dries it
Because air is sinking; it is compressed and warms slightly, so clouds evaporate and skies stay clear
Because high pressure pushes all clouds towards the equator
Because anticyclones only occur in summer
questions.explanation: In an anticyclone air slowly descends. Sinking air warms as it is compressed, so water droplets evaporate and clouds cannot form — giving clear skies and light winds, hot in summer but cold and frosty in winter.

questions.stem: The forecast says 'a fresh northerly wind'. Which way is the wind blowing?
choices: Towards the north
From the north, towards the south
From the south, towards the north
It is not possible to tell
questions.explanation: Winds are named after the direction they blow FROM, not towards. A northerly comes from the north — which is why northerlies bring cold Arctic air to Britain.

questions.stem: Which feature of a city helps create the 'urban heat island' microclimate?
choices: Large lakes cooling the air
Dark roads and buildings absorbing and storing heat, traffic releasing heat, and tall buildings blocking cooling winds
Trees shading every street
The higher altitude of city centres
questions.explanation: Tarmac and concrete store daytime heat and release it at night, vehicles and heating add more, and buildings shelter the city from cooling breezes — so city centres can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around them.

questions.stem: A warm front and then a cold front pass over a town, one after the other. Which sequence of temperature and weather is correct?
choices: Steady rain then milder → brief heavy showers then cooler and clearer
Heavy showers then colder → steady rain then milder
Continuous sunshine throughout
Snow then hail then fog
questions.explanation: A warm front brings gradual cloud and steady rain followed by milder air. The cold front behind it brings a narrow band of short, heavy showers as warm air is forced up sharply, then cooler, brighter, showery air.

questions.stem: Two weather stations record rainfall on the same day. Station A (on the windward side of a hill) records 24 mm; Station B (on the leeward side) records 3 mm. What explains the difference?
choices: Station B's rain gauge must be broken
Moist air rose and rained over the windward slope; the descending air on the leeward side warmed and dried, leaving B in a rain shadow
Station A is nearer the sea, and rainfall always increases closer to the sea
Convectional rainfall only happens on windward slopes
questions.explanation: This is classic relief rainfall. Forced ascent wrings moisture out of the air on the windward side; by the time the air descends to Station B it is warmer and drier, so leeward locations get far less rain — the rain shadow effect.

questions.stem: A gardener notices that frost forms on open lawn but never beside the south-facing brick wall of the house. What is the best explanation?
choices: The wall creates a microclimate: it absorbs heat by day and releases it at night, and shelters the strip from cold winds
Frost only forms on grass, never on soil
The wall attracts more rainfall, which prevents frost
South-facing walls reflect frost back into the sky
questions.explanation: Brick stores solar heat during the day and radiates it overnight, while the wall also shelters the area from wind. This creates a warmer microclimate that keeps the strip frost-free — why gardeners grow tender plants against sunny walls.

questions.stem: A barometer falls steadily from 1015 mb to 985 mb over 24 hours, and isobars on the forecast chart close together. What should you expect?
choices: Settled, sunny, calm weather as high pressure builds
An approaching depression: rising air bringing thickening cloud, strengthening winds and rain
No change — pressure has no effect on weather
Immediate frost and clear skies
questions.explanation: Falling pressure means air is rising — the signature of an approaching low-pressure system (depression). Tight isobars show a steep pressure gradient, so strong winds will accompany the cloud and rain.
